title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Dallas, TX: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Dallas-Fort Worth: study online or host it at your shop, with construction, aerospace and pipeline work in view.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Dallas-Fort Worth: A Six-Day Course for the Metroplex
html:
Dallas-Fort Worth never seems to stop building. Warehouses go up along the interstates, data halls rise on the edges of the suburbs, hospital and office towers keep the tower cranes busy downtown, and the highway program rebuilds interchanges one phase at a time. Out west, aerospace plants in Fort Worth and Arlington weld airframe and engine hardware, and natural gas and liquids pipelines cross the region toward the Gulf Coast. All of it runs on welds that need an inspector's signature. Atlantis NDT runs a six-day course that gets welders, fitters, QC staff, NDT technicians and engineers ready for the AWS Certified Welding Inspector examination. If you are preparing alone, you take it online with a study plan, course materials, practice questions and an instructor who answers your questions. If you are an employer preparing a crew, Atlantis can bring the six days to your shop or yard. Request a Dallas-Fort Worth quote to get started.

Keep the division of roles straight from day one. The examination belongs to AWS, and AWS alone grants the CWI title. Preparation is the whole of Atlantis's role. It has no AWS approval or endorsement, takes no part in setting or marking the exam, and has no view of exam content. Practice material is written in-house against the subject areas AWS publishes, so it trains the same skills without borrowing a single question from AWS.

What drives welding inspection demand across the Metroplex

Most CWI hiring in North Texas follows four streams of work. The largest is commercial and industrial construction, which brings structural steel welding under AWS D1.1 and the special inspection programs that building departments require. The second is transportation: bridges, flyovers, managed lanes and transit structures built for state and local agencies, usually to AWS D1.5. The third is aerospace and defense manufacturing on the west side of the metro, with its own fusion welding specifications and strict traceability. The fourth is energy, centred on pipelines and the compressor stations, meter stations and terminals that connect them. Behind those sit steel fabricators, tank and vessel shops, trailer and equipment builders, and the testing laboratories that supply inspectors to all of them.

Construction steel and special inspection in North Texas

Cities across the Metroplex build under the International Building Code with local amendments, and the code's special inspection chapter applies to structural steel welding. On a typical commercial building, the engineer of record writes a statement of special inspections, the owner hires an independent agency to perform them, and the agency's welding inspector checks shop and field welds against D1.1 and the project drawings. Inspectors on those jobs spend their days confirming welder qualification records, checking joint preparation before welding, watching for undercut, porosity and incomplete fusion, measuring fillet sizes, and writing reports that the building official will read.

Data centres have become a big part of that workload. A data hall is a large steel structure with heavy mechanical systems hung from it, and the projects come with tight schedules and owners who expect clean documentation at turnover. The welding is mostly structural steel plus mechanical piping for chilled water and fuel systems, so inspectors with a D1.1 grounding and some exposure to piping codes are in demand on those sites. Warehouse and distribution projects are simpler steel but very high volume, and they keep fabricators and erectors busy year round.

Texas heat is the local complication, and it works differently from northern winters. Preheat is rarely the problem in August; the inspector's concerns are welders working in exhausting conditions, consumables kept dry in humid storage, and coatings and primers applied to steel that is still too hot. A good inspector watches for low-hydrogen electrodes left out of their ovens on a humid morning, because that is where hydrogen cracking starts.

Bridges and highways: why D1.5 matters here

The Texas Department of Transportation and the regional toll and transit authorities keep a large volume of steel bridge work moving through the Metroplex. Girders and other bridge steel come out of shops working to AWS D1.5, a code AASHTO and AWS publish together. D1.5 is stricter than D1.1 in several ways that matter to an inspector: procedures generally have to be qualified by test rather than relying on prequalified joints, consumable control is tighter, and fracture-critical members carry their own set of extra requirements. Fabrication shops that supply bridge work need inspectors who can enforce those rules in the shop rather than discover problems at the job site.

Because D1.5 (2020 edition) is on the AWS list of Part C books, a bridge-shop welder or QC technician can take the open-book test in the code already open on the desk at work. For candidates who split their time between buildings and bridges, D1.1 is usually the more flexible choice, with D1.5 studied after certification.

Aerospace in Fort Worth and Arlington

The western half of the Metroplex is one of the country's concentrations of military aircraft and rotorcraft manufacturing, supported by a large network of machine shops, weld shops, heat treaters and finishing suppliers. Airframe and engine welds generally follow AWS D17.1 or a prime contractor's specification, and inspection on those parts is more about weld class, acceptance limits and traceable records than about the large structural welds a building inspector sees. Many aerospace suppliers ask their weld inspectors for a CWI because it proves broad welding knowledge, then add their own internal training on the customer's specification.

AWS currently offers D17.1 (2024 edition) as a Part C option, which makes it a sensible choice for a candidate whose career is staying in aerospace. The course's code day covers how D17.1 organizes weld classes, inspection requirements and acceptance criteria. For context on the NDT methods used on aerospace parts, see UT in aviation and PT in aviation.

Pipelines and API 1104 work out of Dallas

Dallas is a headquarters town for the midstream industry, and the Fort Worth Basin's Barnett Shale made the western suburbs familiar with gathering lines, compressor stations and drilling pads long before the current wave of construction. Interstate and intrastate lines run through and around the metro, and pipeline construction crews based in North Texas work across the state and beyond. Transmission and gathering pipeline welding is generally done to API 1104, and federal pipeline safety rules administered by PHMSA incorporate that standard by reference; intrastate lines in Texas are overseen by the Railroad Commission of Texas. Pipeline inspection contractors, operators and construction companies hire welding inspectors for mainline, tie-in and repair work.

AWS offers API 1104 (22nd edition) for Part C. One detail catches candidates out: the federal regulations still incorporate the 21st edition, so a Texas pipeline job may run to an edition different from the one you used for the exam. Learn the 22nd edition well for the test and keep track of what changed between editions afterwards. The article on WPS, PQR and WPQ under ASME IX, D1.1 and API 1104 explains how procedure and welder qualification differ between pipeline and structural work, and the API 1104 standard summary covers the document itself. For the methods that follow visual inspection on pipeline welds, see UT for pipelines.

The AWS exam as a North Texas candidate experiences it

Three separate parts make up the examination, and each must be passed with at least 72 percent. Part A, Fundamentals, has 150 questions; expect processes, metallurgy, mechanical and nondestructive tests, symbols, procedure and qualification documents, safety and the math an inspector uses. Part B, Practical, combines hands-on tasks with 46 questions, using inspection tools on weld samples and working from procedure documents. Part C, Code Application, is open-book and runs 50 to 65 questions in the code book chosen at application.

The computer-based parts, A and C, are booked through Prometric once AWS has accepted the application and issued an eligibility code. Part B is handled by AWS itself at seminar locations, and Texas is well served: AWS currently lists Dallas, Austin, Houston, San Antonio, Corpus Christi and Beaumont among its US CWI seminar cities. A Metroplex candidate can therefore usually sit the practical without leaving the area. Locations and dates change during the year, so confirm them on aws.org before arranging time away from work.

Six days that work for a Dallas candidate or employer

The full plan for each day sits on the national AWS CWI exam prep course page. Briefly, the first two days cover the fundamentals: processes, joint design, A2.4 symbols, A3.0 definitions, metallurgy, mechanical tests, why discontinuities form, safety, and what an inspector is responsible for. The third day builds the measuring and visual-acceptance skills Part B checks. The fourth trains the candidate to find answers fast in the chosen Part C code. On the fifth, candidates sit timed mock papers for A, B and C and go through every wrong answer. The sixth returns to whatever scored lowest, plans exam day and checks the AWS application file.

The online version suits someone who travels with a pipeline spread or works long construction hours: there is no start date and no scheduled class to attend, only material to work through and an instructor to ask when a topic does not click. The on-site version suits a fabricator, testing agency or aerospace supplier with several candidates at once. Atlantis runs the six days at the employer's premises, and on the practical day the group measures real welds from the company's own production with the company's own gauges. Atlantis does not ship replica kits and keeps no classroom anywhere in the Metroplex; for Dallas-Fort Worth groups, the venue is the employer's site.

Two free resources help between study sessions: the NDT practice tests for the testing topics in Part A, and the Practical NDT welding workshop for rehearsing inspection steps on screen. The breakdown of CWI results by part shows where candidates usually struggle.

Checking your eligibility before you apply

AWS QC1 (currently the 2016 edition with Amendment 1) decides who may sit the exam, and it measures eligibility as education plus welding-based work experience. Two Metroplex examples show how it works. A pipe welder with a high school diploma needs five years of welding-based experience before applying. A Dallas College graduate holding the welding associate degree needs two. A bachelor's in welding engineering technology lowers the requirement to one year; engineering or technical coursework toward such a degree lowers it to three; completed trade or vocational courses lower it to four. With schooling that ended at eighth grade the figure is nine years, and below that it is twelve.

The application file includes an employment verification form for the experience claimed, the AWS Visual Acuity Exam Form showing a passed vision examination, and acceptable photo identification. Describe each job in plain terms: what you welded or inspected, which codes the work followed, and for how long. AWS judges what counts. Day six of the course reviews the file, but submitting it, passing the vision examination and paying AWS directly are the candidate's responsibilities. More detail is in the guide to CWI requirements and career impact.

North Texas welding schools and the AWS North Texas Section

AWS members in the region belong to the North Texas Section, part of AWS District 17 along with the Central Texas and East Texas sections. Section meetings and events bring together inspectors, fabricators, educators and suppliers, and they are the easiest place for a future CWI to find people who have recently passed, ask about employers that sponsor candidates, and learn how local technical programs count toward professional development hours.

The trade pipeline starts in the colleges. Dallas College teaches welding at its Eastfield, Mountain View and North Lake campuses and offers credit and workforce certificates along with a Welding Applications associate degree. Graduates of programs like that, after a few years in structural, pipe or production welding, have the education and experience profile AWS looks for. A Dallas College associate degree also lowers the experience AWS requires, which is worth knowing when planning a career rather than a single exam.

After certification: renewal, recertification and NDT

The CWI runs on a nine-year cycle. AWS asks for renewal at years three and six, each time confirming no break of more than two years in practice or employment within the prior three years. Recertification comes at the nine-year mark; retaking Part B and logging 80 professional development hours are two of the ways AWS accepts. Experienced inspectors can later pursue Senior CWI; the SCWI pathway article explains how.

Many Metroplex CWIs add NDT methods because building, bridge and pipeline specifications call for magnetic particle and ultrasonic examination of welds after visual acceptance. Atlantis trains NDT to ASNT SNT-TC-1A; your employer certifies you to its written practice, and the course alone certifies nobody. Natural next steps are VT Level 2 training, UT Level 2 training and the NDT training options for Dallas. API 510, 570 and 653 exam preparation is not something Atlantis offers. If you are weighing those routes, read the comparison of NDT technician and welding inspector careers. Employers who need field inspection rather than training can see weld inspection services in Dallas and magnetic particle testing in Dallas.

Requesting a Dallas-Fort Worth quote

Say whether you are enrolling yourself or several people, what each candidate does now and years of welding-based experience, the intended Part C book (D1.1, D1.5, D17.1 and API 1104 are the usual Metroplex picks), and a target exam window. Employers wanting on-site delivery should add the facility address and whether a meeting room, gauges and production weld samples are available. AWS sets and publishes its exam and seminar charges on aws.org; the CWI exam cost calculator helps you budget for books and travel as well. Send the Dallas request and you will hear back within one business day.

Nearby options include the Houston CWI page, the Tulsa CWI page and the Kansas City CWI page.

faq.q: Where do Dallas-Fort Worth candidates take the CWI practical?
faq.a: AWS gives Part B at its seminar locations, and Dallas is currently on its list of US CWI seminar cities, along with Austin, Houston, San Antonio, Corpus Christi and Beaumont. Parts A and C are computer-based through Prometric. Check aws.org for the current calendar.

faq.q: Which Part C code book suits a bridge fabricator in North Texas?
faq.a: AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code, which AWS currently offers for Part C. Building steel inspectors usually choose D1.1, aerospace candidates D17.1 and pipeline candidates API 1104.

faq.q: Why might my pipeline job use a different API 1104 edition from the exam?
faq.a: AWS uses the 22nd edition for Part C, while the federal pipeline regulations still incorporate the 21st. Learn the 22nd for the exam and check which edition each project specifies.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a CWI classroom in Dallas?
faq.a: No. Its US office is in Houston. Dallas-Fort Worth candidates study online with an instructor answering questions, or their employer hosts the six days at its own facility.

faq.q: How many days is the course?
faq.a: Six. On-site groups normally run them back to back; online candidates work through the same six days of content around their schedules.

faq.q: Do I become a CWI by finishing the course?
faq.a: No. AWS administers the exam and grants the certification. You need to meet the QC1 eligibility rules, pass the AWS vision examination and pass Parts A, B and C.

faq.q: Does an associate degree reduce the experience AWS asks for?
faq.a: Yes. Under AWS QC1, a two-year degree in welding, engineering, engineering technology or physical science cuts the welding-based experience requirement to two years, compared with five for a high school diploma.

faq.q: Can an aerospace supplier in Fort Worth host the course for its weld inspectors?
faq.a: Yes. The six days can run at your facility, D17.1 can anchor the code day, and candidates practise measurement on your own parts with your own gauges. Tell us the number of inspectors and their roles in the quote form, and expect an answer within one business day.

faq.q: Are your practice questions real AWS questions?
faq.a: No. They are original questions written to the subject areas AWS publishes. Real exam content is confidential.

faq.q: What should I study after the CWI if I work around Dallas?
faq.a: Visual testing, then magnetic particle or ultrasonic methods, trained to ASNT SNT-TC-1A with certification from your employer. See NDT training for Dallas.
